319	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
320	
321	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
322	
323	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
324	
325	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
326	
327	```text
328	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
329	```
330	
331	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
332	
333	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
334	
335	```text
336	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
337	```
338	
339	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
340	
341	### Confidence levels, defined
342	
343	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
344	
345	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
346	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
347	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
348	
349	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
350	
351	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
352	
353	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
354	
355	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
356	
357	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
358	
359	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
360	
361	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
362	
363	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
364	
365	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
366	
367	```text
368	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
369	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
370	```
371	
372	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
373	
374	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
375	
376	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
377	
378	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
379	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
380	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
381	
382	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
383	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
384	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
385	
386	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. A chain is also rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites — the stated confidence label of each `Cn` on its head line, the part before the first `→`. This is a ceiling: it bounds the rating from above and is never a reason to rate a chain HIGH, and a cited chain rated MEDIUM under a validation-rubric EXCEPT clause still caps every chain that cites it. Every MEDIUM or LOW confidence line explains only its own chain's rating, so its validity never depends on how far away a cap originates. The line names each `GT-N?` input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. It names each `Cn` on the chain's head rated below HIGH and need not re-explain that `Cn`, whose own confidence line carries the explanation, so no line has to trace a cited chain's lineage. For each downgrade cause belonging to the chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — the line states what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists. A stated reason is the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause; "speculative" is never such a reason. The validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause is the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, and naming any other clause, including the speculative EXCEPT clause, stands in for nothing. A chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing, so the rubric's speculative EXCEPT clause no longer covers it, and the cited chain's own confidence line states its verification path; a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another chain's head, and stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (§5).

410	## 6. Conclusion
411	
412	Summarize the analysis result. The Conclusion section synthesizes what the Derivation Chains established — it does not introduce new claims or reasoning.
413	
414	**Recommended approach:** [Description of the recommended course of action, decision, or design choice.]
415	
416	**Key insight:** [The non-obvious finding the first-principles analysis revealed — what reasoning by analogy or convention would have missed.]
417	
418	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** [What is being accepted, deprioritized, or deferred as a result of this recommendation. No recommendation is free of trade-offs.]
419	
420	**Pre-check:** head [each chain the Conclusion rests on with its band, e.g. C1 (MEDIUM), C3 (HIGH); plus any GT-N? it rests on directly] · ?-marked: [ids, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
421	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
422	
423	If Confidence is MEDIUM or LOW: name each chain contributing to the Conclusion that is rated below HIGH, and each `GT-N?` input the Conclusion rests on directly with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. The line need not restate a named chain's verification path or no-path reason; the named chain's own §4 confidence line carries it. Give any downgrade cause belonging to the Conclusion itself with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists, as §4 defines. A MEDIUM or LOW conclusion without this explanation does not satisfy D-07.
424	
425	**Claim inventory.** A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
426	
427	**Citation form.** Every Conclusion-section claim either names the chain that established it inline — `(chain C1)` — or is discharged by a §6→§4 closure ledger row that quotes the claim and names its chain. A claim doing neither is cut, not softened. Ledger discharge requires the structural row form the closure-ledger example below shows — a list marker, then the quoted claim, then an arrow, then the chain id — and a prose sentence that merely quotes something and names a chain is not a ledger row. This is detected only when the row sits inside section 6: the ledger emitted as process output before the analysis is not visible to the check, and inline citation is therefore the mechanically checkable form.
428	
429	**Conforming — inline chain citation:**
430	
431	```text
432	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate (chain C1).
433	```
434	
435	**Conforming — closure-ledger row:**
436	
437	```text
438	- "Move sustained workloads to Fargate" → chain C1 ✓
439	```
440	
441	**Non-conforming — a claim naming no chain and quoted by no ledger row:**
442	
443	```text
444	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate.
445	```
446	
447	Both forms are accepted because both discharge the same obligation: the ledger is process output emitted before the analysis (see the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions"), not a seventh output section, and the chain IDs cited are the `C1`/`C2` IDs assigned by §4's chain-numbering convention.
448	
449	**Caveats.** A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
450	
451	**Not a claim — a bold lead-in alone on its line, carrying no citation:**
452	
453	```text
454	**Recommended approach — three steps, in this order:**
455	```
456	
457	This is the hinge of "detectable from the emission alone" — an author can dodge extraction by putting the lead-in on its own line, and the claim obligation then falls to the numbered items beneath it.
458	
459	**A claim — the same lead-in carrying its assertion on the same line:**
460	
461	```text
462	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate before evaluating Lambda (chain C1).

125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.

130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.

135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.

140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading

356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
357	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
364	
365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.
374	
375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents
389	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
390	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
391	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
392	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
393	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
394	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
395	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
396	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token;
397	  and every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by
398	  arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity
399	  cited to an unsuffixed ground truth — the test `output-template.md` states for the HIGH
400	  band under "Confidence levels, defined", shared here rather than restated. A hop that
401	  follows once the `[Assumes: X]` premise declared on that hop is granted counts as following
402	  for this criterion — declaring the premise takes the hop out of this limb by design, and
403	  whether that premise is priced is Criterion 5's Inference axis. An undeclared premise is not
404	  treated that way: a hop the endpoint depends on whose only gap is an undeclared premise is a
405	  non-sequitur under Hand-wavy below, and the `[Assumes: X]` limb above covers undeclared
406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.
448	
449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.
612

entries.description:
- Allows Claude to search the web and use the results to inform responses
- Provides up-to-date information for current events and recent data
- Returns search result information formatted as search result blocks, including links as markdown hyperlinks
- Use this tool for accessing information beyond Claude's knowledge cutoff
- Searches are performed automatically within a single API call

CRITICAL REQUIREMENT - You MUST follow this:
  - After answering the user's question, you MUST include a "Sources:" section at the end of your response
  - In the Sources section, list all relevant URLs from the search results as markdown hyperlinks: [Title](URL)
  - This is MANDATORY - never skip including sources in your response
  - Example format:

    [Your answer here]

    Sources:
    - [Source Title 1](https://example.com/1)
    - [Source Title 2](https://example.com/2)

Usage notes:
  - Domain filtering is supported to include or block specific websites
  - Web search is only available in the US

IMPORTANT - Use the correct year in search queries:
  - The current month is September 2026. You MUST use this year when searching for recent information, documentation, or current events.
  - Example: If the user asks for "latest React docs", search for "React documentation" with the current year, NOT last year

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

Links: [{"title":"Communication in the context of long-distance family caregiving: An integrated review and practical applications - ScienceDirect","url":"https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0738399110005240"},{"title":"PROXIMITY, CARE VALUES, AND CAREGIVING STRAIN: EVIDENCE FROM THE 2020 NAC/AARP NATIONAL SURVEY","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11692659/"},{"title":"PRELIMINARY EFFICACY OF A MULTICOMPONENT INTERVENTION DESIGNED FOR LONG-DISTANCE FAMILY CAREGIVERS","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11690640/"},{"title":"Caregiver Burden And Caregiving Benefits in Long-Distance Family Caregivers","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12762539/"},{"title":"Residential Proximity and Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety Among Adult Children Caring for Aging Parents","url":"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12759417/"},{"title":"PROXIMITY, CARE VALUES, AND CAREGIVING STRAIN: EVIDENCE FROM THE 2020 NAC/AARP NATIONAL SURVEY - PMC","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11692659/"},{"title":"Long-Distance Caregiving Guide | AgeWays Michigan","url":"https://www.ageways.org/2026/07/01/long-distance-caregiving-supporting-an-aging-parent-from-afar/"},{"title":"Long-Distance Caregiving: How To Support Aging Parents From Afar","url":"https://www.humangood.org/resources/senior-living-blog/long-distance-caregiving-how-to-support-aging-parents-from-afar"},{"title":"Family Caregiving from a Distance: A New and Understudied Trend | The LeadingAge LTSS Center @UMass Boston","url":"https://www.ltsscenter.org/family-caregiving-from-a-distance-a-new-and-understudied-trend/"}]

I found comprehensive research on long-distance caregiving effectiveness and caregiver burden compared to proximity-based caregiving. Here are the key findings:

## Caregiving Burden Differences

Proximal caregivers experience more objective burden (time, effort, tasks, and money), while distance caregivers experience more subjective burden (perceptions, attitudes, and emotions regarding caregiving).

Recent research presents interesting findings on physical and financial strain: Caregivers providing care at a distance reported lower physical and financial strain levels, though long-distance carers who live more than one hour away show more physical and financial strain than those living with or close to their parents.

## Types of Care Provided

Instrumental activities for daily living (IADL) for elderly parents such as meal preparation, home maintenance, and shopping tend to require more proximity. The farther away geographically, the less likely a sibling was expected to and actually provided care.

## Emotional and Mental Health Impact

Long-distance caregivers of persons with dementia experience significant caregiving burden and strains similar to geographically close caregivers. Additionally, close to 50% of long-distance caregivers helping an older adult with significant cognitive impairment living in the community reported levels of burden, depression, and anxiety that were higher compared to long-distance caregivers with care recipients living in a nursing home.

## Research Gap

Almost all existing research has focused on geographically close caregivers, and evidence-based interventions were designed and tested with proximate caregivers, not considering the unique circumstances of long-distance family caregivers.

# Study Findings on Proximity and Caregiving Strain

The research reveals a nuanced relationship between residential distance and caregiver burden:

**Physical and Financial Strain:**
"Long-distance carers, namely those who live more than one hour away from their parents, show more physical strain (b=-0.236, p< 0.05) and financial strain (b =-0.228, p< 0.05) than those who live with or close to their parents."

**Emotional Strain (Unexpected Finding):**
The study found that caregivers living close to parents reported lower emotional strain, but this pattern reversed for long-distance caregivers, who showed a positive (though statistically insignificant) relationship with emotional strain—contradicting prior research.

**Care Values as a Stronger Predictor:**
More striking than proximity was caregivers' perceived choice in providing care. "Whether the respondents feel they had a choice to take care of their parents is a statistically significant predictor of physical (b=0.508, p< 0.05), financial (b=0.446, p< 0.05), and emotional strain (b=0.810, p< 0.05)."

This suggests that subjective perceptions about autonomy in caregiving may matter more than objective distance in predicting strain.

content.content:
# Study Findings on Moving and Educational Outcomes

## Key Finding
Children who frequently move homes or schools have significantly worse early educational achievement. The study analyzed 121,422 Welsh children's formal assessments at ages 6-7.

## Effect Sizes

**Residential Moves:**
- Three or more moves between ages 1-4: adjusted odds ratio (OR) of 1.16 for not achieving
- Two or more moves between ages 4-6: adjusted OR of 1.16 for not achieving
- Moves before age 1 showed no significant effect

**School Moves (Strongest Effect):**
- Two or more school moves: adjusted OR of 2.33—over twice the odds of not achieving

The research notes "only 78% of children with at least two residential moves between the ages of 4 and 6 achieved ks1 compared to 87% in those who did not move."

## Key Moderators

1. **Timing matters**: Moves during ages 4-6 (school years) had greater impact than earlier moves
2. **School changes matter more**: School moves showed dramatically larger effects than residential moves alone
3. **Socioeconomic factors**: Free school meal eligibility and area deprivation significantly influenced outcomes

The authors conclude that "school moves had a much larger effect" than residential mobility on early educational attainment.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Holmes-Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale:

## Overview

The Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS), often known as the Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale, was developed by Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe in 1967. The scale was designed to identify major stressful life events and was based on the premise that such events, regardless of whether they're positive or negative, might necessitate significant adjustment and, hence, induce stress.

## Structure and Scoring

The SRRS comprises a list of 43 stressful life events, ranging from marriage and divorce to minor law violations and changes in sleeping habits. Each of the 43 life events was awarded a Life Change Unit, depending on how traumatic it felt to be by a large sample of participants.

For example, "Death of a spouse" has the highest LCU value of 100, indicating it's the most stressful event on the list.

## Score Interpretation

By adding up the LCUs of events an individual has experienced over a year, one can get a score that predicts the likelihood of experiencing a major health breakdown in the subsequent two years. 150 points or less means a relatively low amount of life change and a low susceptibility to stress-induced health breakdown, while 150 to 300 points implies about a 50% chance of a major health breakdown in the next 2 years.

GT-1 is *not* `?`-marked — it was read at source — but it rests on one national survey (2020 NAC/AARP), a real single-study limitation distinct from unverified-provenance. If a differently-designed study found distance itself, independent of choice, to be the dominant strain predictor, C1 and the part of C4/C5 built on it would need to be reweighted toward "closer is just better, full stop." Weakest links per chain: **C1** — GT-3 (reported-by-delegate, not opened at source); **C2** — the literature's largest effect size is reported for "two or more" moves, and no isolated odds ratio for a single planned move by a financially stable family was located in the source read; **C3** — GT-5 (reported-by-delegate); **C4** — inherits C1–C3's caps by citation; **C5** — GT-4 and GT-8 both reported-by-delegate/unverified, and the A10/A11 assumption-hops are not fully priced.

**Rival:** Headline rival — *"Just move; family bonds matter more than any of this optimization, and you can't calculate your way to a good family decision."* This is **not ruled out** — it is a legitimate terminal-value claim, not a factual one, and first-principles analysis has no instrument for adjudicating terminal values. It is carried live into §5 (Dead End 2) and into the Conclusion's caveat rather than argued away. Per-chain rivals: **C1** — "paid help fully substitutes IADL support, so proximity has zero care value" — not settled (GT-6 shows paid help is costly and availability-dependent, not a clean substitute, but this isn't conclusively ruled out here). **C2** — "even one move still carries meaningful risk because the isolated single-move effect size wasn't found" — live, unsettled, named in C2's confidence line. **C3** — "the asymmetry is really just about who earns more, not portability" — addressed/subsumed by GT-11's multi-factor decomposition (licensure, market thickness, remote-compatibility, tenure — not salary alone), so this rival doesn't survive as a distinct alternative. **C4** — "a formal weighted procedure is overkill for a family decision" — not ruled out; the object-level point (fix the criteria and their priority before comparing options) is argued to survive even if done informally rather than numerically. **C5** — "the stress effects are generic to any big life change, not specific to relocating for parents" — true, and it sharpens rather than overturns C5's claim (the point is the *stacking*, not novelty).

**Adversarial technique — pre-mortem (the analysis's Recommended Approach is a plan, so pre-mortem applies, not inversion):**

*Premise:* It is three years after a naive, proximity-only relocation (no structured plan, no portability check, no consent check). The move has already failed — the family is worse off on career, marriage, or children's wellbeing than had they stayed, with no compensating gain in the parents' actual care outcomes. What caused it?

*Causes (unfiltered, from three stakeholder viewpoints):*
Trailing-career-spouse viewpoint: (1) job search took far longer than budgeted, depleting savings; (2) licensure/credentials didn't transfer, forcing a lower-tier role; (3) they never really agreed, just acquiesced to avoid conflict; (4) new role pays materially less with no path back to prior seniority; (5) lost their own professional/social network with nothing rebuilt.
Children's viewpoint: (6) a child mid-way through a specialized program (IEP, gifted track, exam-year curriculum) had no destination equivalent; (7) the move landed mid-school-year; (8) the children absorbed an unplanned support/caregiving role themselves; (9) household conflict from cause (3) raised the stress the kids lived inside.
Ageing parent's viewpoint: (10) the parent didn't actually want the increased proximity — it produced friction/loss of autonomy, not closeness; (11) the parent's needs escalated into a stage (e.g., dementia) where institutional/professional care became necessary anyway, and the proximity rationale evaporated after the cost was already sunk; (12) a sibling already local resented the newcomer or a turf conflict over caregiving roles emerged.
Structural: (13) nobody ever defined what "helping" concretely meant operationally; (14) cost-of-living in the destination was mispriced, straining finances; (15) the decision was made reactively during a health scare with no contingency planning.

*Clusters (each named, each citing what it bears on):*
- **Cluster A — "proximity mistaken for a plan"** (causes 10, 11, 13) → bears on C1, GT-12, precondition P6.
- **Cluster B — "uncosted/unequal career sacrifice"** (causes 1, 2, 4, 5) → bears on C3, GT-5, GT-11, precondition P2.
- **Cluster C — "non-consensual decision"** (causes 3, 9) → bears on C5 (marital 2nd/3rd-order hops), precondition P7.
- **Cluster D — "mismatched developmental/logistical timing"** (causes 6, 7) → bears on C2, GT-2, precondition P3.
- **Cluster E — "family-system role realignment"** (causes 8, 12) → bears on GT-3, C1, C5.
- **Cluster F — "financial miscalculation"** (causes 14, 15) → bears on GT-6, precondition P5.

*Disposition:*
- A — **Fatal.** Plan change: require an explicit, written caregiving operating plan (who does what, how often, escalation triggers) as a precondition of relocating; without one, proximity delivers co-location, not care.
- B — **Fatal-to-costly.** Plan change: require a per-partner portability assessment before commitment; a non-portable career with no acceptable compensation routes the family toward a non-full-relocation option instead.
- C — **Fatal.** Plan change: require both partners' independently-elicited, explicit consent as a precondition; passive acquiescence does not count.
- D — **Costly but survivable.** Mitigation: time the move to a natural school transition point and confirm continuity of any specialized program before committing.
- E — **Costly but survivable.** Mitigation: negotiate caregiving-role division with local siblings in writing before moving.
- F — **Costly but survivable.** Mitigation: build a destination cost-of-living-adjusted budget and a minimum 6–12 month financial runway before either resignation is submitted.

*Falsification:* The Conclusion below is false if raw geographic proximity — independent of need-type match, plan concreteness, portability-adjusted career cost, and mutual consent — is itself shown to be the dominant, sufficient driver of good family and eldercare outcomes.

- **GT-2** In a Welsh cohort of 121,422 children (assessed ages 6–7), two or more school moves between ages 4–6 carried an adjusted odds ratio of 2.33 for not achieving expected Key Stage 1 attainment (78% vs 87% achievement); residential-only moves carried a much smaller adjusted OR of 1.16; moves before age 1 showed no significant effect; school moves showed a substantially larger effect than residential moves, moderated by deprivation/free-school-meal eligibility — source: PLOS ONE cohort study; read-at-source: [journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0070601](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0070601), results section, quoted directly via WebFetch.

# 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: Proximity does not reliably "produce better care" as a general claim

GT-1 (choice beats distance as a strain predictor) + GT-3? (IADL support needs proximity) + GT-9 (travel-time floor on emergency response) + GT-12 (need-type sets the minimum-sufficient intervention)
→ perceived choice in caregiving is a stronger predictor of strain than raw distance, so "closer" does not uniformly reduce strain for caregiver or care-recipient
→ the tasks that genuinely require physical co-location are a narrow subset of possible needs — routine IADL support and time-sensitive emergency response — not the full range of what "ageing parent needs" can mean *[Assumes: A8]*
→ relocating produces a real care benefit only when the parents' actual need falls in that narrow subset, and no generic analysis can determine whether it does — the family must establish this fact first

### Conclusion C2: The "changing schools harms children" rule overstates the risk of a single, planned, financially-stable move

→ a family able to execute one deliberate, well-resourced, one-time move without repeating it or destabilizing its finances is not drawn from the population driving the large effect sizes above *[Assumes: A6]*
→ blanket "don't uproot the kids" reasoning conflates a high-instability population's average outcome with a single-move, stable-family case, and materially overstates the risk for the latter — though the risk is not zero if the move is poorly timed or becomes one of several disruptions

# 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Replace "closer = more caring" with a four-gate, five-criterion decision procedure the family runs on its own facts before either job is given notice (chains C1, C2, C3, C4). The gates and criteria:
- Confirm the parents' actual need-type on the spectrum from relational-only to 24/7 custodial
- Confirm each partner's career portability separately, not as one shared number
- Confirm the destination can match any specific school program a child currently depends on
- Confirm 6–12 months of financial runway exists before any resignation
- Confirm both partners' independently-elicited consent, not passive agreement
- Confirm the parents' own consent to increased involvement
- Write the caregiving operating plan (who, what, how often, escalation) before moving, not after
- Tripwire: no concrete recurring caregiving routine exists six months post-move
- Tripwire: the less-portable partner has no comparable job by the pre-agreed runway date
- Tripwire: either partner privately says they wouldn't choose this again within year one

**Key insight:** The variable that actually separates good outcomes from bad ones is not distance but whether the family can name a concrete, jointly-owned care plan matched to the parents' real need-type, priced against portability-adjusted career cost and school-timing risk — the failure mode observed across the pre-mortem's causes is not "moving" or "not moving," it is mistaking proximity itself for the plan (chains C1, C5).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This analysis explicitly declines to produce a universal "move" or "stay" verdict, deprioritizing false precision in favor of naming the scoring procedure itself as the deliverable (chain C4); it also accepts a LOW-confidence extension (chain C5) on the marriage/long-run-acuity effects because the underlying empirical inputs there are unverified or reported-by-delegate. Wanting to be near ageing family for its own sake, independent of any instrumental caregiving benefit, is a legitimate value this analysis has no authority to weigh for the family — no chain — flagged assumption only.
